verse.text: Paul, a slave of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, for the faith of God’s chosen ones and the knowledge of the truth that accords with godliness,
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, not a hired servant. Most English versions soften it to “servant,” though several recent ones print “slave.” In the Greek Scriptures “slave of the Lord” was also an honorific for figures such as Moses and David, so the title conveys both total belonging and a commissioned role.

The preposition can mean “in accordance with” or can express purpose or direction. On the reading chosen here, Paul’s apostleship exists to serve the faith and knowledge of God’s chosen people; on the other, his apostleship conforms to that faith. Most recent translations and commentators take it as purpose.

verse.text: in the hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised long ages ago

note.traditional: before the world began; before the ages began

verse.note: The Greek is literally “before long ages” or “before age-long times,” using the plural of the word for a stretch of time with the adjective elsewhere rendered “eternal.” Many versions paraphrase as “before the world began” or “before time began,” taking the promise as made before creation; others understand a promise made in the distant past. The same adjective in “eternal life” in this verse refers in Jewish usage to the life of the age to come, a matter of kind as well as length.

verse.text: and at the proper time he revealed his word in the proclamation with which I was entrusted by the command of God our Savior,
to Titus, my true child in the faith we share: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.
This is why I left you in Crete: so that you would set right what was left undone and appoint elders in every town, as I directed you:
someone who is beyond reproach, the husband of one wife, with believing children who are not open to a charge of wild living and are not rebellious.
verse.note: The Greek is literally “a man of one woman.” It has been understood as excluding polygamy, as excluding remarriage after divorce or after a wife’s death, or more generally as requiring marital faithfulness (“faithful to his wife”). The wording does not settle the question, and scholars remain divided.

The adjective can mean “believing” (that is, sharing the faith) or “faithful, trustworthy.” Most translations take it as “believing,” but some scholars argue that it means dependable and well-behaved children, which fits the description that follows.

verse.text: For an overseer, as God’s household manager, must be beyond reproach—not arrogant, not quick-tempered, not given to wine, not violent, not out for shameful gain,
verse.note: The Greek word means someone who watches over or supervises, and was used for various officials and guardians. Older English versions render it “bishop,” the word that descends from it, but that suggests the later office of a single bishop over a region. Here the “overseer” appears to be the same figure as the “elders” of verse 5, as most scholars hold, though some see the beginnings of a distinct role.

verse.text: but hospitable, a lover of what is good, sensible, righteous, devout, self-controlled,
holding firmly to the faithful word as it has been taught, so that he may be able both to encourage with sound teaching and to rebuke those who speak against it.
For there are many who are rebellious, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision,

note.traditional: they of the circumcision; the circumcision party

verse.note: The phrase refers to people of Jewish background, here evidently Jewish believers in Jesus within the Cretan congregations. It may also carry the idea that they were pressing Jewish observances on others, which fits the mention of “Jewish myths” and human commands in verse 14.

verse.text: who must be silenced. They are overturning whole households, teaching what they should not for the sake of shameful gain.
One of them, a prophet of their own, said, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.”
verse.note: The line is a verse of Greek poetry that ancient writers attributed to Epimenides, a Cretan sage of several centuries earlier who was regarded as an inspired figure. The reputation of Cretans as liars was proverbial in the Greek world. The last phrase is literally “idle bellies.”

verse.text: This testimony is true. For this reason rebuke them sharply, so that they may be sound in the faith,
not paying attention to Jewish myths and the commands of people who turn away from the truth.
To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure; rather, both their mind and their conscience are defiled.

note.term: To the pure all things are pure

verse.note: “Pure” and “defiled” are the vocabulary of ritual cleanness, especially in rules about food and contact. The statement answers the opponents’ “commands of people” in verse 14, which probably included purity regulations. The point is that purity is a matter of the person, not of the things handled or eaten.

verse.text: They profess to know God, but by their works they deny him; they are detestable, disobedient, and unfit for any good work.
But as for you, speak what is fitting for sound teaching.
Older men are to be sober, dignified, sensible, sound in faith, in love, and in endurance.
verse.note: This word family runs through the chapter (verses 2, 4, 5, 6 and 12) and is rendered with “sensible,” “good sense” and “sensibly” so the repetition can be heard. It named a prized Greek virtue: sound judgment that keeps impulses in check. Many versions use “self-controlled,” which is a fair gloss but is also the usual rendering of a different Greek word.

verse.text: Older women likewise are to be reverent in their bearing, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, teachers of what is good,
verse.note: The adjective means “befitting what is sacred” and was used of people and conduct connected with temples and priestly service. The suggestion is that older women should carry themselves as people engaged in holy service.

verse.text: so that they may teach the young women good sense—to love their husbands and their children,
to be sensible, pure, busy at home, kind, submitting to their own husbands, so that the word of God may not be slandered.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read a rare word meaning “working at home”; many later ones read a commoner word meaning “staying at home” or “keeping house,” which lies behind the King James “keepers at home.” The following adjective, “good,” is taken here as a separate quality (“kind”), but it can be joined to this word to give “good homemakers.”

The Greek verb meant defamatory speech against anyone or anything, not only irreverence toward God. Here the object is the Christian message, which outsiders would speak ill of if believers behaved badly, so “slandered” is used. Several versions keep “blasphemed” or use “reviled” or “maligned.” The “slanderers” of verse 3 translates a different Greek word.

verse.text: Likewise urge the younger men to be sensible.
In everything show yourself a model of good works: in your teaching, integrity, dignity,

note.traditional: in all things shewing thyself a pattern

verse.note: The Greek phrase stands between the two sentences and could end verse 6 (“to be sensible in everything”) instead of beginning verse 7. The translation follows the punctuation of the Greek edition used and most English versions.

verse.text: and sound speech that is beyond reproach, so that the opponent may be put to shame, having nothing bad to say about us.
Slaves are to submit to their own masters in everything, to be pleasing to them, not talking back,
verse.note: The word refers to people owned by a master, a normal part of households in the Roman world, and “servants” in older versions softens this. Most modern translations use “slaves.” The instruction addresses how believers in that position should act; it does not discuss the institution itself.

verse.text: not pilfering, but showing complete and genuine faithfulness, so that in everything they may adorn the teaching of God our Savior.
verse.note: This is the same Greek word rendered “faith” in verse 2. Set against pilfering, it means the quality of being trustworthy, so “faithfulness” is used. The Greek is literally “showing all good faithfulness.”

verse.text: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all people,
verse.note: The verb, and the related noun “appearing” in verse 13, were used in the Greek world for the visible manifestation of a god or the arrival of a ruler to help his people. The two occurrences frame the present life between Christ’s first appearing and his awaited one.

note.traditional: that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men

verse.note: “To all people” can go either with “bringing salvation,” as here and in most modern versions, or with “has appeared,” as in the King James Version. The word order favors the first.

verse.text: training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires and to live sensibly, justly, and with godliness in the present age,
verse.note: Greek has one word family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice). The adverb here describes conduct that is right and fair toward others, and “justly” is used. Most versions have “righteously” or “upright.”

verse.text: as we wait for the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ,

note.term: our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ
note.traditional: the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ

verse.note: The Greek can be read as naming one person, Jesus Christ, who is called both God and Savior, or two, “the great God” and “our Savior Jesus Christ.” Most modern translations and grammarians favor the first because a single article governs both nouns and “God and Savior” was a set phrase in the period, but the second remains possible. A third view takes “Jesus Christ” as explaining “the glory” of God.

verse.text: who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people of his own, eager for good works.
verse.note: The phrase echoes the Greek Old Testament, where God calls Israel his special possession among all nations (for example Exodus 19:5 and Deuteronomy 7:6). “Peculiar” in older English meant “belonging exclusively to,” not “odd.”

verse.text: Speak these things, and urge and rebuke with full authority. Let no one disregard you.
Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work,
to slander no one, not to be quarrelsome, to be considerate, showing all gentleness toward all people.
verse.note: The Greek verb is the source of English “blaspheme,” but in the first century it meant abusive or defamatory speech against anyone, human or divine. Here the object is people, so “slander” is used. Older versions have “speak evil of,” and modern ones vary among “slander,” “malign” and similar words.

Older versions have “meekness,” which now suggests weakness or timidity. The Greek word describes a humble, unassertive manner toward others, with no implication of feebleness. “Gentleness” or “humility” is the usual rendering in modern translations.

verse.text: For we too were once senseless, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various desires and pleasures, passing our lives in malice and envy, detestable, hating one another.
But when the kindness and love for humanity of God our Savior appeared,
verse.note: The Greek word is philanthrōpia, a virtue that the Greek-speaking world regularly praised in gods, kings and public benefactors. The language of a savior whose kindness “appeared” would have reminded readers of how such rulers were honored. Here that language is applied to God.

verse.text: not on the basis of works that we ourselves had done in righteousness, but in keeping with his mercy, he saved us through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit,
verse.note: “Righteousness” here and “justified” in verse 7 translate words from a single Greek family, which English splits between “righteous” and “just.” The link is deliberate: people are not saved by right deeds of their own but are set right by God’s grace. Some scholars prefer “justice” for the noun throughout.

note.term: the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit
note.traditional: the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost

verse.note: The Greek can be read as one washing that brings both rebirth and renewal, all of it the Spirit’s work. It can also be read as two things, a washing of rebirth and a renewal by the Holy Spirit. The translation leaves both readings open. Most interpreters see a reference to baptism in “washing,” though some take it as a purely figurative cleansing.

verse.text: whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior,
so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs in keeping with the hope of eternal life.
verse.note: The Greek adjective is formed from the word for “age.” In Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, so the phrase speaks of the kind of life as well as its unending length. “Eternal” is the standard rendering; a minority of translators prefer “life of the age to come.”

verse.text: The saying is trustworthy, and I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have put their trust in God may take care to devote themselves to good works. These things are good and profitable for people.
verse.note: The Greek adjective is normally rendered “faithful” in this translation. Applied to a saying, it means reliable or deserving of trust, and “faithful” is not natural English for that, so “trustworthy” is used. The formula recurs in the letters to Timothy and Titus. Here it most likely points back to the summary of salvation in verses 4–7.

note.traditional: be careful to maintain good works

verse.note: The Greek phrase, repeated in verse 14, could also mean “engage in honorable occupations,” that is, earn an honest living. The verb can mean to take the lead in something, to busy oneself with it, or to practice a trade. Most translations and commentators take it as devotion to good deeds, which suits the letter’s repeated stress on good works.

verse.text: But avoid foolish debates and genealogies and strife and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable and futile.
After a first and second warning, have nothing more to do with a divisive person,
verse.note: The Greek word is the source of English “heretic,” and older versions use that word. In the first century it described someone who forms factions or causes divisions. The sense of holding condemned doctrine developed later. Most modern translations have “divisive” or “factious.”

verse.text: knowing that such a person is warped and is sinning, being self-condemned.
When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, do your best to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there.
verse.note: Several cities bore this name, which means “city of victory.” Most scholars identify this one with Nicopolis in Epirus, on the western coast of Greece, a port where a traveler could reasonably wait out the winter when sea travel stopped.

verse.text: Do your best to send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way, so that they lack nothing.
verse.note: In the Gospels this word names experts in the Law of Moses. Zenas has a Greek name and nothing more is known of him, so he may have been a jurist in Roman or Greek law or a Jewish legal expert. Commentators are divided, and “lawyer” leaves the question open.

The Greek verb means more than saying goodbye. It was the usual term for equipping travelers with food, money and whatever else they needed for the next stage of a journey, as the following clause, “so that they lack nothing,” makes clear.

verse.text: And let our people also learn to devote themselves to good works to meet pressing needs, so that they will not be unfruitful.
All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with all of you.
